paragraphs: I was given the opportunity to do a clinical study abroad in America and the UK for about four months, from February 22 to June 23. Of that, for the first four weeks, with the support of the Medical Education Promotion Foundation, I trained in neurology at the University of Glasgow; for the next six weeks in pulmonology and infectious diseases at Duke University, which has a partnership with Nagoya University; and for the last six weeks in obstetrics and gynecology at the University of Cambridge. Before I knew it, I had ended up doing clerkships at three places, and the application was also very hard, but with great help I was able to finish safely. I would like to describe each below.

The first place I went was Glasgow, a city in Scotland in the north of the UK. I studied in neurology at Queen Elizabeth University Hospital, the hospital affiliated with the University of Glasgow here. The University of Glasgow has produced the economist Adam Smith and James Watt, who invented the steam engine, and it is also the place where Masataka Taketsuru, founder of Nikka Whisky, familiar from the NHK morning drama "Massan," studied abroad. As for medicine, its neurology field is famous as the place where the GCS (Glasgow Coma Scale) was devised. Besides me, students from Gunma University, Juntendo University and Hamamatsu University School of Medicine were dispatched by the foundation, so we worked hard while exchanging information about the content of our respective clerkships. What was especially impressive was that there were many patients with multiple sclerosis, which is rare in Japan. Furthermore, I was surprised that there was even a specialised outpatient clinic for multiple sclerosis. Also, on days off I was truly glad to be able to meet again people who had come to Nagoya University for clinical clerkships from the University of Glasgow and the University of Edinburgh in the past.

The next place I went was Durham, North Carolina, in America. After a week of travelling in the northeast, I trained here at Duke University for four weeks in pulmonology and two weeks in infectious diseases. In pulmonology, the first, I was able to see patients with cystic fibrosis, again something rare in Japan. As for infectious diseases, it had originally not been possible to go, but through the connection of Jenny, my host mother who looked after me again this year, I was able to train there as an observership. For me, who am interested in infectious diseases, being able to form a rough image of infectious diseases departments in America was a very valuable experience. Also, partway through, in Greensboro, a little away from Durham, I was allowed to observe anesthesiology under Dr. Kaori Longphre, an alumna of the Frontier Association. On days off too I experienced many things unique to America and enjoyed myself to the full.

The last destination was Cambridge in England. This place has no partnership with the foundation or the university, but I applied almost solely out of the wish to attend once again a college formal dinner just like in Harry Potter, triggered by having been allowed to go to St John's College, Cambridge, on a university-wide exchange for only two weeks when I was a second-year student. The clerkship department was obstetrics and gynecology, but because the doctor in charge specialised in gynecologic oncology and the content of the clerkship was more substantial, gynecology became the main part. Outside the clerkship, a medical student from Johns Hopkins who had come to Nagoya University last year in the same program took me to that formal dinner, and because the timing overlapped, I went with other exchange students to the end-of-year ball hosted by the colleges, called the May Ball. On days off I also enjoyed walking around Cambridge, and going a little further to France I was able to watch the French Open tennis tournament.

Unfortunately, I did not feel that my English greatly improved or my knowledge increased through this experience, but I think it was very meaningful in that I was able to learn about the differences in medical care and medical education between the two countries, America and the UK, and even the differences in medical English, and that I met many people who support, and will support, Japan within the world. Overall, America was all new to me, but in the UK I was very glad to be able to meet various people again. Finally, I would like to express my deep thanks to Dean Dr. 門松, Dr. 粕谷 of the International Collaboration Office, Dr. 長谷川, Dr. Itzel and all the other doctors. In particular, Dr. 長谷川 was a great help during the application procedures. Thank you.
